vignette:
Mele is a 75-year-old woman of Oceania descent, a retired auditor who still works part-time reviewing ledgers for a small firm. She is married and lives with her husband in a quiet suburban home. Decades ago, during a period of civil unrest in her home country, Mele was caught in a violent ambush while walking to a market. She remembers the chaos—the sharp crack of gunfire, the screams, and the suffocating press of bodies around her. What she recalls most vividly, however, is the smell: the acrid sweat of the man pressed against her, the metallic tang of blood, and the sour body odour of the wounded. She can still see the scene like a series of photographs in her mind—a man’s face contorted in fear, a broken fruit cart, the sun glinting off a discarded weapon. Yet when she tries to put it into words for her therapist, the descriptions evaporate. She knows what happened, but the language to describe it escapes her, like trying to catch smoke.

In the years since, Mele has lived with a quiet dread. She avoids feeling happy or relaxed, because those moments of ease are now reliably punctured by the sudden return of that olfactory recall—sweat, body odour, the smell of the crowd. A colleague’s perfume or the scent of a gym bag in the office hallway can trigger a cascade of images, and she finds herself back in that alley, seeing the photographs in her mind. These triggers also awaken her deepest negative appraisals. When she catches a whiff of sweat, she feels exposed, as though others can see her trauma written on her face. She has come to believe that she will never feel normal emotions again, that the woman she was before is gone. This sense of permanent damage makes her question whether her life is still worth living, though she has never acted on the thought.

Her memory of the event, so visual and sensory, drives her to ruminate endlessly. She goes over and over why it happened to her, what she could have done differently. She replays the minutes before the ambush, trying to find a moment where she might have turned back, might have prevented it. This rumination, in turn, reinforces her negative appraisals—the more she turns the event over in her mind, the more convinced she becomes that she is fundamentally broken. It also feeds her threat perception. The photographic clarity of the memory makes her feel unsafe in any space where she cannot see the entire room. She always sits with her back to a wall. At work, she frequently looks behind her to check if someone is following her, even down the empty corridors of the accounting office. She has also begun taking too many risks—driving too fast, walking through unsafe neighbourhoods at dusk—as if daring the world to prove her fears right. Each time she rehearsed a conversation or ate lunch alone in the storage room, her nervous system logged the effort as proof that the world was dangerous—if she had to work that hard to stay safe, the threat must be real and still out there, waiting.

Her maladaptive strategies extend beyond rumination. Before any interaction, even a simple conversation with a colleague, Mele rehearses what to say, running through every possible response. This preparation is exhausting, but she cannot stop. It is her way of controlling a world she feels has already betrayed her. Yet the rehearsing itself triggers more memories—the anticipation of failure loops back to the helplessness of the ambush. And the fact that she still needed to do all of this—the rehearsing, the isolating, the constant scanning—confirmed, in some wordless way, that she wasn't getting better, that she must be more broken than she had let herself believe. The cycle tightens. The more she rehearses, the more she feels exposed to others’ scrutiny, and the more she scans for threats. She has started isolating herself at work, eating lunch alone in a storage room where she can sit with her back to the wall, away from the smell of the break room.

What finally brought Mele to seek help was a moment at the office last month. She caught a whiff of sweat from a delivery man and, for a moment, she was back in the alley, her heart pounding, her breath shallow. She excused herself to the bathroom and cried, unable to stop. Her husband noticed she had stopped smiling at home, that she flinched when he touched her. She came to therapy because she is afraid of what she might do next—not just the risky behaviours, but the quiet thought that maybe her life is not worth living anymore. She hopes, dimly, that someone can help her find the words she has lost.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals: No paragraph conveys that Mele's maladaptive strategies (rehearsing, isolating) cause or reinforce her negative appraisals (e.g., feeling broken).
  e.g. "Three years of avoiding it had told her something she couldn't easily argue with: that she must be more fragile than other people, or she would have been over this by now."
  e.g. "Each time she used a safety behaviour to get through the day, she felt the quiet accumulation of evidence that she couldn't cope without it."
  e.g. "The fact that she still needed to do all of this — the checking, the planning, the long way round — confirmed, in some wordless way, that she wasn't getting better."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Threat: No paragraph conveys that Mele's maladaptive strategies (rehearsing, isolating) cause or increase her sense of threat.
  e.g. "Never having stayed in a situation long enough to find out it was safe, her body had never received the evidence it needed — the threat remained as high as the day it was set."
  e.g. "The checking and the avoidance had kept her alive, in her nervous system's accounting, which meant the danger they were responding to must be real and ongoing."
  e.g. "Without ever testing the feeling, she had no way to know that the threat was not what her body insisted it was — the safety behaviours had sealed that possibility off."
